title: Wall Street Banks Push Big Law to Cut Fees Because of AI
pub: Financial Times (reported via Point Blank and Startup Fortune)
author: Financial Times · Point Blank · Ron Patel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source accepts that AI-driven time savings do not mechanically reduce firm profits and materially develops the cluster’s account of the mediating forces. It identifies rate increases as one firm response, while documenting demand growth, staffing and AI-adoption costs, and mounting buyer pressure over who captures efficiency gains.
qs: The early response from many firms has been to raise the rate on the hours that remain, rather than give clients a clean discount on hours removed.
Bloomberg Law separately reported in August 2026 that demand grew 4.2% in the first half of the year, while firms faced rising costs from the talent fight and the race to adopt AI.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that corporate buyers are pressing to capture AI gains and that this pressure is challenging time-based billing. It materially extends the synthesis with concrete examples of bank invoice scrutiny and an Australian firm restructuring its practices around AI-resistant versus AI-enabled work, while not demonstrating realised fee reductions or quantified savings.
qs: They want the savings on the invoice.*  Goldman Sachs has started asking outside counsel a specific question: how much is AI actually saving you on our matters?

kp.k: Banks demand a share of AI efficiency savings
kp.d: Both articles relay Financial Times reporting that Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup are pressing outside law firms to change fees as AI accelerates routine work. Goldman reportedly asks firms to quantify savings on its matters and uses those answers in negotiations. These are reported client demands, not evidence of achieved fee reductions.
qs: Goldman is using the answer in fee negotiations, pressing firms to quantify AI-driven efficiency and share part of the benefit with the bank.
Morgan Stanley and Citigroup are pushing in the same direction, asking major law firms to rethink what they charge when software has sped up research, document review and contract analysis.

kp.k: Client leaders challenge hourly economics and firm leverage
kp.d: Point Blank frames AI as challenging the leverage model built on junior lawyers billing for research, review and discovery. It quotes Citigroup global head of legal Adam Meshel's conditional expectation that fewer AI-assisted hours should substantially reduce transaction costs, and Morgan Stanley general counsel Eric Grossman's criticism of BigLaw's compensation model. Neither quotation establishes that this model has already collapsed.
qs: Firms have long billed hourly for armies of junior lawyers grinding through research, document review and discovery.
“If the number of hours they’re working on a matter has come down because of AI… our expectation is for costs to come down significantly per transaction,”
“extraordinarily unstable.”

kp.k: Routine junior tasks accelerate, but human checking remains
kp.d: Patel describes contract review and due diligence as routine, text-heavy tasks in which AI can perform a first pass previously undertaken by junior lawyers. He expressly retains lawyer checking of the result. The claimed speed improvement is an explanatory assertion, without a measured productivity study or quantified verification burden.
qs: A junior lawyer once had to sit with the documents, flag terms, compare clauses and feed the findings up the chain.
Now a machine can do a first pass in minutes, even if a lawyer still has to check the result.

kp.k: Surveys report expectations of reduced hourly billing
kp.d: Patel cites Wolters Kluwer's 2024 Future Ready Lawyer Survey: 67% of corporate legal departments and 55% of law firms expected AI efficiencies to affect the prevalence of the billable hour. He reports that its 2026 survey found 62% of legal department respondents and 57% of law firm respondents expected significantly reduced reliance on billable hours. These are expectations, with differently worded outcomes, rather than observed billing changes; the document supplies no sample sizes.
qs: Wolters Kluwer's 2024 Future Ready Lawyer Survey found that 67% of corporate legal departments and 55% of law firms expected AI-driven efficiencies to affect the prevalence of the billable hour.
Its 2026 survey went further, with 62% of legal department respondents and 57% of law firm respondents saying AI would significantly reduce reliance on billable hours.

kp.k: High junior billing rates sharpen clients' pricing objections
kp.d: Patel cites Bloomberg Law's 2023 reporting on bankruptcy court filings: one first-year Sullivan & Cromwell associate in the FTX bankruptcy was billed at $1,310 an hour, while lawyers graduating in 2021 were often billed at $960 an hour. He uses these historical examples to explain client resistance if AI reduces first-pass review time, not as evidence of AI-related rate reductions.
qs: Bloomberg Law reported in 2023 that one first-year Sullivan & Cromwell associate on the FTX bankruptcy case was billed at $1,310 an hour, while lawyers who graduated in 2021 were often billed at $960 an hour.
Those were bankruptcy court filings, not a theoretical pricing sheet.

kp.k: Alternative pricing remains experimental and uneven
kp.d: Patel reports experimentation with fixed fees, competitive bidding, subscriptions and value-based pricing, alongside continued hourly billing. His assertion that firms cannot indefinitely avoid the pricing dispute is a prediction rather than an observed market outcome.
qs: The replacement model is still messy.
Some firms are testing fixed fees for defined work. Others are using competitive bidding, subscriptions or value-based pricing for repeat work.
Many are still billing by the hour and hoping the argument stays vague enough to survive another budget cycle. It won't.

kp.k: Australian firms change billing and internal performance measures
kp.d: Point Blank reports Australian adoption of alternative fee arrangements as AI use accelerates. Attributing the claim to the AFR, it identifies Keypoint Law as the only local firm to have abandoned the billable minute entirely. DLA Piper's Australian arm reportedly prioritises fees generated rather than hours logged in a performance measure. These organisational changes do not establish that clients are paying less, a question the article explicitly raises.
qs: In Australia, pricing models are starting to shift, but are clients actually paying less?
ditch the billable minute entirely
Australian arm has introduced a “performance measure” that prioritises fees generated, instead of just hours logged.

kp.k: Firm restructuring separates corporate and AI-powered procedural work
kp.d: Point Blank reports that Thomson Geer split into Thomsons and Faculti, distinguishing a practice pursuing work characterised as AI-resistant from an AI-powered practice for procedural matters. The document identifies insurance and leasing as examples but supplies no performance results for the split.
qs: **Thomsons**, chasing AI-resistant, top-tier corporate work, and **Faculti**, an AI-powered practice built for procedural, process-driven matters like insurance and leasing.

kp.k: Firms counter efficiency pressure with higher hourly rates
kp.d: Patel asserts that many firms initially respond by increasing rates on remaining hours instead of passing through a clear discount. He conditions the strategy's viability on continued client willingness to pay and interprets Goldman's questioning as evidence of declining patience; no quantified rate-response study is provided.
qs: The early response from many firms has been to raise the rate on the hours that remain, rather than give clients a clean discount on hours removed.
That strategy works only while clients keep paying.

kp.k: Revenue growth coexists with rising staffing and technology costs
kp.d: Patel cites Citi's Law Firm Group and Hildebrandt Consulting reporting 11.3% revenue growth, 1.9% demand growth, 9.1% expense growth and 2.9% headcount growth in the first nine months of 2025, alongside strong opening inventory and a more senior, expensive lawyer mix. He separately cites Bloomberg Law's August 2026 report of 4.2% demand growth in the first half of 2026 and rising talent and AI-adoption costs. These figures contextualise firms' resistance to discounts rather than isolate AI's financial effects.
qs: Citi's Law Firm Group and Hildebrandt Consulting reported that law firm revenue grew 11.3% in the first nine months of 2025, helped by 1.9% demand growth and strong inventory entering the year.
Expenses rose 9.1% over the same period, with headcount up 2.9% and firms leaning into a more senior and expensive lawyer mix.
Bloomberg Law separately reported in August 2026 that demand grew 4.2% in the first half of the year, while firms faced rising costs from the talent fight and the race to adopt AI.

kp.k: AI investment creates a dispute over savings allocation
kp.d: Patel frames the central economic tension as clients demanding technology investment, lawyer training and faster delivery while seeking the resulting savings, whereas firms bear licensing costs and prefer margin improvements. The document leaves unresolved whether benefits should accrue to firms, clients or both.
qs: Clients want firms to buy the tools, train lawyers on them and move faster. Then they want the savings handed back at the negotiating table.
Firms, meanwhile, are paying the licensing bills and would rather treat AI as margin, not a rebate.
Someone has to decide whether AI savings belong to the firm that bought the tool, the client that paid for the work, or both.

kp.k: Buyer pressure may spread across professional services
kp.d: Patel argues that the banks' buying power makes demands for savings difficult to ignore and recommends that consulting and accounting firms take notice. He analogises legal review to structured work such as standard audit testing, cites FT reporting of existing pressure on consulting fees for IT projects and system integration, and predicts wider procurement demands. The broader spread is his forecast, distinct from the reported consulting negotiations.
qs: Goldman, Morgan Stanley and Citi have the buying power to make the question expensive for law firms to ignore.
Consulting and accounting firms should pay attention.
The FT reported the same day that companies are already pushing consultants to lower fees as AI reduces the need for outside work on areas such as IT projects and system integration.
Once procurement teams learn the question works with law firms, they'll ask it everywhere.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The articles report that banks are demanding a share of AI efficiencies through lower legal fees, and argue that AI pressures hourly billing, junior-heavy staffing economics and the allocation of law-firm profits.
pts.d: Point Blank and Ron Patel, reporting on the Financial Times, describe Goldman Sachs asking outside counsel to quantify AI savings for fee negotiations, with Morgan Stanley and Citigroup also seeking changed payment arrangements. Citigroup's Adam Meshel explicitly conditions his expectation of significantly lower transaction costs on AI reducing matter hours. Morgan Stanley's Eric Grossman describes BigLaw's compensation model as extraordinarily unstable. Point Blank asserts that AI performs routine research, document review and discovery faster and more cheaply, challenging the associate-to-partner leverage model. Patel describes AI as producing a first pass of document work in minutes, while retaining lawyer verification. He argues that these efficiencies expose hourly billing and that firms will not be able to defer pricing pressure indefinitely. He reports experiments with fixed fees, competitive bidding, subscriptions and value-based pricing, alongside firms raising rates on remaining hours rather than passing through straightforward discounts. Point Blank reports Australian shifts toward alternative fees and fees-generated performance measures, and describes Thomson Geer's split into Thomsons for AI-resistant top-tier corporate work and Faculti for AI-powered procedural work. Patel also predicts that similar client pressure will spread across consulting and accounting.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of reported client negotiations and executive statements, surveys of expectations, illustrative billing records, law-firm financial data and examples of organisational change—not measured AI savings on the banks' matters.
pts.d: Both accounts rely on Financial Times reporting for bank demands; Point Blank reproduces Meshel's conditional cost expectation and Grossman's assessment. Patel cites Wolters Kluwer surveys: in 2024, 67% of corporate legal departments and 55% of firms expected AI efficiencies to affect the prevalence of hourly billing; in 2026, 62% of legal department respondents and 57% of firm respondents expected significantly reduced reliance on billable hours. These are reported expectations, not observed fee reductions. Patel cites Bloomberg Law's reporting of bankruptcy filings showing a first-year Sullivan & Cromwell associate billed at $1,310 an hour on FTX and lawyers graduating in 2021 often billed at $960 an hour. These illustrate prices rather than AI's causal effect. He cites Citi's Law Firm Group and Hildebrandt Consulting for 11.3% revenue growth, 1.9% demand growth, 9.1% expense growth and 2.9% headcount growth in the first nine months of 2025, and Bloomberg Law for 4.2% demand growth in the first half of 2026. These contextualise firms' economic position and costs. Point Blank cites reporting on Australian alternative fee arrangements, an AFR account identifying Keypoint Law as the only local firm to abandon billable minutes entirely, DLA Piper's changed performance measure and the Thomson Geer split. No task-level benchmark, quantified bank-matter saving or confirmed client discount is supplied. The expectation that pricing pressure will become unavoidable and spread more widely is authorial argument, supported in the consulting case by additional FT reporting.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The accounts portray fee pressure and pricing experiments as current on 1 September 2026; wider displacement of hourly billing and diffusion to other services remain prospective and without a specified deadline.
pts.d: Both articles are dated 1 September 2026. Patel says general counsel offices had been asking about savings for a couple of years, with major banks' buying power now making those demands harder to ignore. The survey evidence covers expectations reported in 2024 and 2026; the financial context covers the first nine months of 2025 and the first half of 2026. Meshel's requested cost reduction depends on AI actually reducing hours per matter. Patel qualifies automation as a first pass requiring lawyer checking, not autonomous completion of the whole legal service. He says remaining-hour rate increases work only while clients accept them, and acknowledges that firms must pay licensing and training costs. The replacement pricing model remains unsettled, and the articles do not establish that clients have already received lower invoices. Point Blank explicitly asks whether Australian pricing changes are producing actual savings. Patel's prediction of wider procurement pressure has no dated endpoint.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern powerful corporate legal buyers and major outside law firms, with distinct implications for junior work, Australian practice segments and adjacent professional-service providers.
pts.d: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Citigroup are buyer-side institutions seeking lower transaction costs and a share of productivity gains. Their general counsel offices and procurement functions are presented as using purchasing power to change pricing. Big Law firms face pressure on hourly revenue and junior-heavy leverage while bearing AI licensing, training and talent costs; Patel frames the dispute as whether efficiency becomes firm margin or a client rebate. Junior lawyers' research, review, discovery, due diligence and contract-analysis tasks are described as susceptible to faster AI first passes, but the source does not quantify job losses or predict a specific staffing reduction. Lawyers remain responsible for checking results. In Australia, Keypoint Law and DLA Piper illustrate billing or performance-measure changes, while Thomsons and Faculti illustrate differentiation between top-tier corporate work described as AI-resistant and process-driven insurance and leasing work. Patel extends the argument to consultants and accountants whose structured work supports existing fee models. The source focuses on enterprise purchasing, not access to justice for individuals or small organisations.
